html:
A research team from Tsinghua University, the University of Cambridge and ByteDance has recently proposed a new method that lets large language models (LLMs) understand spatial audio. Today’s multimodal models can only make sense of ordinary audio; this work gives an LLM a first, rudimentary ability to “hear” the direction and position of sounds in three-dimensional space.

The study is built around three core tasks: sound source localization (SSL), far-field speech recognition (FSR) and localization-informed speech extraction (LSE).

  • Sound source localization. The team took a novel approach: they fed spatial feature vectors derived from four-channel spatial audio into the LLM’s input, allowing the model to judge the angle of a sound source accurately. On the Spatial LibriSpeech dataset the model brought the mean angular error down to 2.7°, a marked improvement on the 6.6° of the previous baseline.

  • Far-field speech recognition. With the spatial features added, the model’s word error rate also dropped further, showing that an LLM can use spatial information to understand speech better.

  • Localization-informed speech extraction. Given an instruction, the model can single out and extract the sound coming from a specified direction, and it still does this well when several people are talking at once and their speech overlaps.

On the methods side, the team froze both the widely used Whisper speech encoder and the LLM, and fine-tuned only the alignment module that connects the two, along with a few selected layers. Spatial information was injected at an intermediate layer of the model, which worked better than fusing it in at the end. The researchers also found no extra benefit in adding direction angles to the model’s vocabulary as dedicated special tokens.

To give the LLM material for learning spatial perception and separating multiple sources, the team also synthesized a large amount of complex spatial audio using realistic room-acoustics simulation. Taken together, the experiments show that LLMs have real potential for understanding spatial hearing and perceiving complex 3D scenes, and they hint at a future in which AI enters the real world as a listening agent.

The work supplies a key link in moving LLMs from “only hearing what is said” to “understanding real space,” and it lays the groundwork for future agents that perceive and interact within virtual or real three-dimensional environments.
